categories.title: Cerebrovascular System
categories.description: Comprehensive study of carotid and vertebral artery anatomy, physiology, and pathology

topics.title: Carotid Anatomy & Normal Values
topics.quickSummary: The ICA supplies the brain (low resistance), while the ECA supplies the face/scalp (high resistance). Understanding these differences is critical for exam success.
clinicalPearls: Carotid exam performed with patient supine, neck slightly extended, head turned away from side being scanned
ICA = Internal Carotid Artery (low resistance vessel)
ECA = External Carotid Artery (high resistance vessel)
Vertebral arteries evaluated as part of cerebrovascular assessment
70-99% carotid stenosis is a CRITICAL FINDING requiring immediate attention
Linear array transducer used for carotid exams

sections.title: ICA vs ECA Characteristics
sections.content:
ICA (Internal Carotid Artery): Low resistance vessel supplying brain. Continuous forward diastolic flow throughout cardiac cycle. Longer acceleration time. PI < 1.0 is normal.

ECA (External Carotid Artery): High resistance vessel supplying face/scalp. Minimal or reversed diastolic flow. Similar pattern to resting extremity arteries.

sections.title: Normal Values
sections.content:
ICA has increased acceleration time (AT) compared to high resistance vessels due to low resistance
AT longer in ICA and cerebral vessels vs extremity arteries
Brain vessels: Pulsatility Index (PI) normally <1.0
ICA waveform: low resistance with continuous forward diastolic flow
ECA waveform: high resistance with minimal/reversed diastolic flow

keyTakeaways: ICA = low resistance (brain needs constant perfusion)
AT longer in ICA than extremities

topics.title: Carotid Scanning Technique
topics.quickSummary: Proper positioning and technique are crucial. The most common error causing underestimation of stenosis is improper sample volume placement.
clinicalPearls: Most common reason for underestimation of carotid stenosis = improper sample volume location
Cursor should be placed at narrowest point of stenosis initially
Move Doppler cursor through entire stenotic area to find highest velocity
Bruit can be heard with stenosis, also with branching/tortuosity
Patient supine with neck slightly extended
Head turned away from side being scanned
Scan entire length of CCA, ICA, ECA, and vertebral arteries

sections.title: Patient Positioning
sections.content:
Patient supine with neck slightly extended
Head turned away from side being scanned
Linear array transducer
Scan entire length of CCA, ICA, ECA, and vertebral arteries
Multiple angles through stenosis to find peak velocity
Doppler angle ≤60 degrees
Sample volume centered in vessel at narrowest point

sections.title: Critical Technique Points
sections.content: MOST IMPORTANT: Move Doppler cursor through ENTIRE stenotic area to find highest velocity. Don't rely on single measurement. Doppler angle must be ≤60 degrees. Sample volume centered in vessel at narrowest point initially, then scan through entire stenosis.

keyTakeaways: Supine, neck extended, head turned away
MUST scan entire stenosis for peak velocity
Most common error: improper sample volume placement

topics.title: Carotid Stenosis & Critical Findings
topics.quickSummary: 70-99% carotid stenosis is a CRITICAL FINDING. Understanding stenosis criteria and hemodynamic changes is essential.
clinicalPearls: Carotid stenosis: 50% diameter = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant
Increased PSV and EDV at stenosis site
Post-stenotic turbulence (eddy currents/vortices) distal to stenosis
50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant
70-99% stenosis = critical finding requiring immediate attention
ICA/CCA velocity ratio helpful for grading stenosis

sections.title: Hemodynamic Significance
sections.content:
50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant threshold.

At stenosis: Increased PSV and EDV, spectral broadening.
Distal to stenosis: Post-stenotic turbulence with eddy currents and vortices.

sections.title: Critical Findings
sections.content:
70-99% stenosis = CRITICAL FINDING requiring immediate physician notification.

Velocity criteria help grade severity. ICA/CCA ratio useful for normalizing cardiac output effects.

keyTakeaways: Increased PSV and EDV at stenosis
ICA/CCA ratio normalizes for cardiac output

categories.title: Arterial Hemodynamics
categories.description: Understanding waveform patterns, resistance, and hemodynamic principles

topics.title: Triphasic Waveform
topics.quickSummary: NORMAL pattern for resting extremity arteries. High resistance vascular bed with three phases: forward, reverse, forward.
clinicalPearls: Late diastole: small amount of forward flow
Seen in high resistance vascular beds (extremities/muscles)

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.content:
Normal extremity arterial waveform

Systole: rapid antegrade flow
Early diastole: retrograde flow
Late diastole: small amount of forward flow
Seen in high resistance vascular beds (extremities/muscles)
Normal in healthy extremity arteries

sections.title: Significance
sections.content: Indicates healthy high resistance vascular bed. Normal in extremities/muscles at rest. Seen in ECA. Would be ABNORMAL in organ vessels.

keyTakeaways: Three phases: systolic forward, early diastolic reverse, late diastolic forward

topics.title: Biphasic Waveform
topics.quickSummary: Indicates mild disease OR medium resistance. Can be normal in older patients but ABNORMAL if seen in organ vessels.
clinicalPearls: Diastole: some retrograde flow (less than triphasic)
Loss of late diastolic forward component
Can be normal in older patients
ABNORMAL if seen in organ vessels

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.content:
Mild disease or medium resistance

Systole: antegrade flow
Diastole: some retrograde flow (less than triphasic)
Loss of late diastolic forward component
Can be normal in older patients
ABNORMAL if seen in organ vessels

sections.title: Clinical Significance
sections.content:
Mild disease or vasoconstriction effect

Two components: systolic forward flow and some diastolic reverse flow (less than triphasic). Loss of late diastolic forward component.

keyTakeaways: Biphasic = mild disease OR medium resistance
Can be normal in older patients

topics.title: Monophasic Waveform
topics.quickSummary: NORMAL for organs (continuous perfusion needed). ABNORMAL for extremities (indicates significant proximal disease).
clinicalPearls: Antegrade flow continues through entire cardiac cycle
Normal in vessels feeding organs (low resistance)
ABNORMAL if seen in extremity arteries

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.content:
Low resistance or significant proximal disease

Antegrade flow continues through entire cardiac cycle
No retrograde component
Rounded, dampened appearance
Normal in vessels feeding organs (low resistance)
ABNORMAL if seen in extremity arteries

sections.title: Normal vs Abnormal
sections.content:
Normal for organs, ABNORMAL for extremities (indicates significant proximal disease or vasodilation)

NORMAL: ICA, renal, mesenteric, hepatic arteries (organs need constant flow).
ABNORMAL: Extremity arteries (indicates proximal disease or vasodilation).

keyTakeaways: Monophasic = NORMAL for organs, ABNORMAL for extremities
Continuous forward flow, no reverse component
Context determines if normal or pathologic

topics.title: Tardus Parvus Waveform
topics.quickSummary: Indicates SEVERE proximal stenosis/occlusion. Tardus = delayed upstroke. Parvus = decreased amplitude.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.content:
TARDUS (slow): Delayed systolic upstroke
PARVUS (small): Decreased amplitude

Delayed systolic upstroke (tardus = slow)
Decreased amplitude (parvus = small)
Rounded peak
Prolonged acceleration time

sections.title: Clinical Significance
sections.content:
Indicates severe proximal stenosis or occlusion

Seen DISTAL to severe stenosis or occlusion. Prolonged acceleration time (AT). Rounded peak instead of sharp peak. Dampened, low-amplitude appearance.

topics.title: High vs Low Resistance
topics.quickSummary: High resistance = extremities/muscles (triphasic). Low resistance = organs (monophasic). Vasoconstriction increases, vasodilation decreases resistance.
clinicalPearls: Triphasic waveforms with retrograde diastolic flow
Minimal or no forward diastolic flow
Clenching fist increases distal resistance and pulsatility in proximal arteries
Supplies organs needing constant blood flow
Monophasic waveforms with continuous forward flow
Examples: ICA, renal, mesenteric, hepatic arteries

sections.title: High Resistance
sections.content:
Supplies extremities/muscles at rest.

Supplies extremities/muscles at rest
Triphasic waveforms with retrograde diastolic flow
Minimal or no forward diastolic flow
Examples: ECA, resting limb arteries
Vasoconstriction increases pulsatility
Clenching fist increases distal resistance and pulsatility in proximal arteries

sections.title: Low Resistance
sections.content:
Supplies organs needing constant blood flow.

Supplies organs needing constant blood flow
Monophasic waveforms with continuous forward flow
Significant diastolic flow component
No flow reversal
Examples: ICA, renal, mesenteric, hepatic arteries
Vasodilation decreases pulsatility

sections.title: Physiologic Effects
sections.content:
Vasoconstriction: changes monophasic to biphasic/triphasic
Vasodilation: changes triphasic to monophasic
Cold patient: vasoconstriction increases arterial resistance
Warm patient: vasodilation decreases arterial resistance
Exercise: vasodilation in muscles, increased flow
Fist clenching: increases resistance, more pulsatile proximally
Upon fist release: resistance drops, pulsatility reduced, flow increases

topics.title: PSV & EDV Measurements
topics.quickSummary: Both PSV and EDV INCREASE at stenosis due to continuity principle. If EDV = 0, then RI = 1.0.
clinicalPearls: Increases at stenosis site due to body maintaining blood volume
Measured at narrowest point of stenosis
Velocity increases as vessel diameter decreases
Continuity principle: flow volume remains constant
Low in high resistance beds, higher in low resistance

sections.title: Peak Systolic Velocity (PSV)
sections.content:
Increases at stenosis site due to body maintaining blood volume
Measured at narrowest point of stenosis
Velocity increases as vessel diameter decreases
Continuity principle: flow volume remains constant

sections.title: End Diastolic Velocity (EDV)
sections.content:
Increases at stenosis site
If EDV = 0 cm/s, then RI = 1.0
Reflects downstream resistance
Low in high resistance beds, higher in low resistance

sections.title: Continuity Principle
sections.content: Flow volume = Area × Velocity (constant). As vessel diameter decreases at stenosis, velocity must increase to maintain constant flow volume.

keyTakeaways: EDV = velocity at end of diastole

topics.title: Cardiac Output Effects
topics.quickSummary: Cardiac function affects ALL arterial velocities systemically. Velocity ratios help normalize for cardiac output variations.
clinicalPearls: Decreased cardiac function = decreased output = reduced peak arterial velocities
Increased cardiac function = increased output = increased peak arterial velocities
Cardiac output affects all arterial velocities systemically
Velocity ratios help normalize for cardiac output variations

sections.title: Cardiac Impact
sections.content:
Decreased cardiac function = decreased output = reduced peak arterial velocities
Increased cardiac function = increased output = increased peak arterial velocities
Cardiac output affects all arterial velocities systemically
Velocity ratios help normalize for cardiac output variations

sections.title: Clinical Application
sections.content: Use velocity RATIOS (ICA/CCA, renal/aortic) to normalize for cardiac output. Compare bilateral vessels. Both affected equally by cardiac function, so ratios remain valid.

keyTakeaways: Decreased cardiac output = decreased velocities everywhere
Increased cardiac output = increased velocities everywhere
Velocity ratios normalize for cardiac variations
Compare bilateral vessels to identify true disease

categories.title: Arterial Anatomy
categories.description: Comprehensive arterial anatomy of upper and lower extremities

topics.title: Lower Extremity Arterial Anatomy
topics.quickSummary: Sequential pathway: Aorta → Iliacs → CFA → SFA/Profunda → Popliteal → Tibials. SFA is most common site of PAD.
clinicalPearls: Aorta → Common Iliac → External Iliac → CFA → SFA and Profunda → Popliteal → Anterior/Posterior Tibial and Peroneal
CFA = Common Femoral Artery (palpable in groin)
SFA = Superficial Femoral Artery (most common PAD site)
Profunda = deep femoral, important collateral source

sections.title: Arterial Sequence
sections.content:
Abdominal aorta
Common iliac arteries
External iliac artery
Common Femoral Artery (CFA)
Superficial Femoral Artery (SFA)
Profunda femoris (deep femoral)
Popliteal artery
Anterior tibial artery
Posterior tibial artery
Peroneal (fibular) artery

sections.title: Normal Characteristics
sections.content:
Triphasic waveforms in healthy extremity arteries
Higher resistance than organ vessels
Pulsatility Index increases with distance from aorta
Velocities decrease distally

sections.title: Positioning
sections.content:
Supine or semi-erect (if breathing problems/vertigo/back pain)
Knee slightly bent, leg abducted for medial aspect access
Decubitus/lateral for popliteal fossa and posterior calf access
Patient positioning affects hemodynamics

keyTakeaways: Aorta → Iliacs → CFA → SFA/Profunda → Popliteal → Tibials

topics.title: Upper Extremity Arterial Anatomy
topics.quickSummary: Subclavian → Axillary → Brachial → Radial/Ulnar. Respiratory effects OPPOSITE of lower extremities.
clinicalPearls: Subclavian → Axillary → Brachial → Radial and Ulnar
Inspiration: INCREASED flow (opposite of lower extremity)

sections.title: Arterial Sequence
sections.content:
Subclavian artery
Axillary artery
Brachial artery
Radial artery
Ulnar artery

sections.title: Respiratory Effects
sections.content:
Flow affected by respiration
Inspiration: increased flow toward heart
Expiration: decreased flow
Opposite of lower extremity pattern

categories.title: Arterial Disease
categories.description: Stenosis, occlusion, aneurysms, and arterial disease manifestations

topics.title: Stenosis Hemodynamics
topics.quickSummary: 50% diameter = 75% area = hemodynamically significant. Proximal: dampened. At stenosis: high velocity. Distal: turbulence.
clinicalPearls: 50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant

sections.title: Hemodynamic Significance
sections.content:
50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant
Shape and degree of stenosis
Diameter of stenosis
Length of stenosis
Contour (smooth vs rough)
Distal peripheral resistance
Pressure gradient across stenosis
Presence/absence of collaterals
Compounding factors from other diseases

sections.title: Effects of Stenosis
sections.content:
Proximal to stenosis: dampened flow velocity with increased resistance
At stenosis: increased velocity (blood escaping stenotic area)
Proximal and distal: increased velocities detected
Post-stenotic turbulence (eddy currents/vortices)
Pressure drop at stenosis with increased velocity (Bernoulli effect)
Flow volume drop at stenosis
Decreased resistance and velocity distal to stenosis

keyTakeaways: Bernoulli effect: pressure drops at stenosis

topics.title: Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)
topics.quickSummary: Arterioles already maximally dilated at rest with stenosis. Cannot dilate further with exercise → ankle pressure DROPS (abnormal).
clinicalPearls: Arterioles already dilated at rest when stenosis present
Ankle pressure drops with exercise in PAD
Ischemic symptoms in muscles during exercise

sections.title: Pathophysiology
sections.content:
Arterioles already dilated at rest when stenosis present
Exercise cannot further reduce resistance
Ankle pressure drops with exercise in PAD
Reduced ABI calculation
Ischemic symptoms in muscles during exercise

sections.title: Findings
sections.content:
Decreased or absent pulses
Monophasic waveforms distally
Tardus parvus waveforms distal to severe stenosis
Reduced velocities throughout
Spectral broadening at stenosis
Post-stenotic turbulence

keyTakeaways: Arterioles maximally dilated at rest with PAD

topics.title: Arterial Aneurysms
topics.quickSummary: Permanent focal dilation >50% normal diameter. TRUE = all 3 layers. PSEUDO = contained rupture. Splenic artery aneurysm = CRITICAL.
clinicalPearls: True aneurysm: involves all 3 vessel layers
Pseudoaneurysm: contained rupture with fibrous capsule
Saccular: affects one side of vessel wall

sections.title: Definition & Types
sections.content:
Permanent focal dilation of artery >50% normal diameter

True aneurysm: involves all 3 vessel layers
Pseudoaneurysm: contained rupture with fibrous capsule
Fusiform: affects entire circumference
Saccular: affects one side of vessel wall

sections.title: Critical Findings
sections.content:
Splenic artery aneurysm = CRITICAL
Aneurysm rupture = CRITICAL
AAA rupture = surgical emergency

topics.title: Acute vs Chronic Occlusion
topics.quickSummary: ACUTE = CRITICAL FINDING (no collaterals, 6 P's, emergency). CHRONIC = NOT critical (collaterals develop, gradual onset).
clinicalPearls: 6 P's: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia
NOT critical due to collateral circulation

sections.title: Acute Occlusion
sections.content:
Acute arterial occlusion = CRITICAL FINDING
No time for collateral formation
Sudden onset ischemia
6 P's: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia
Requires immediate intervention

sections.title: Chronic Occlusion
sections.content:
Chronic obstruction allows collateral development
NOT critical due to collateral circulation
Gradual onset symptoms
Better tolerance than acute

keyTakeaways: Acute: no collaterals, 6 P's, severe ischemia

topics.title: Spectral Broadening
topics.quickSummary: Widening of spectral waveform. LAMINAR = clear window. TURBULENT = filled window. Stenosis most common pathologic cause.
clinicalPearls: Improper sample volume location near wall

sections.title: Causes
sections.content:
Stenosis (most common)
Tortuosity
Improper sample volume location near wall
Increased sample size
Bifurcations
Turbulent flow

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.content:
Laminar flow = narrow bandwidth, clear spectral window
Turbulent flow = wide bandwidth, filled spectral window
Post-stenotic turbulence causes spectral broadening

keyTakeaways: Laminar flow: narrow bandwidth, clear window
Turbulent flow: wide bandwidth, filled window
Technical: improper sample volume, oversized gate

categories.title: Venous Hemodynamics
categories.description: Understanding venous flow characteristics, respiratory phasicity, and valve function

topics.title: Venous Flow Characteristics
topics.quickSummary: Spontaneity in large veins. Respiratory phasicity (opposite in upper vs lower extremity). Cardiac pulsatility ABNORMAL in lower extremity (indicates CHF).
clinicalPearls: Should be present in CFV, femoral, popliteal veins
Calf veins and saphenous veins normally do NOT demonstrate spontaneity
Flow moves from high to low pressure
Lower extremities - Inspiration: decreased intrathoracic pressure, increased intra-abdominal pressure → decreased flow

sections.title: Spontaneous Flow
sections.content:
Flow detected without augmentation
Should be present in CFV, femoral, popliteal veins
Calf veins and saphenous veins normally do NOT demonstrate spontaneity
Absence indicates obstruction

sections.title: Respiratory Phasicity
sections.content:
Flow moves from high to low pressure
Lower extremities - Inspiration: decreased intrathoracic pressure, increased intra-abdominal pressure → decreased flow
Lower extremities - Expiration: increased intrathoracic pressure, decreased intra-abdominal pressure → increased flow toward heart
Upper extremities - Inspiration: increased flow toward heart
Upper extremities - Expiration: decreased flow
Loss of phasicity suggests proximal obstruction

sections.title: Cardiac Pulsatility
sections.content:
Ripples from adjacent cardiac contraction
Causes turbulent flow in upper vena cava, upper arms, hepatic veins
NORMAL in upper extremities and hepatic veins
ABNORMAL if seen in lower extremities = indicates CHF (Congestive Heart Failure)
Suggests elevated right atrial pressure

keyTakeaways: Spontaneity should be present in CFV, femoral, popliteal
Lower extremity: inspiration decreases, expiration increases flow
Cardiac pulsatility in lower extremity = ABNORMAL (CHF)

topics.title: Augmentation & Reflux
topics.quickSummary: Augmentation tests patency. Reflux >0.5-1.0 seconds indicates valve incompetence. Must evaluate reflux in STANDING position.
clinicalPearls: Tests patency between compression site and probe
Retrograde flow lasting >0.5-1.0 seconds indicates incompetence

sections.title: Augmentation
sections.content:
Manual compression increases flow
Tests patency between compression site and probe
Tests valve competence
Brisk augmentation = normal
Blunted/absent augmentation = obstruction

sections.title: Reflux
sections.content:
Retrograde flow lasting >0.5-1.0 seconds indicates incompetence
CFV: >0.5 seconds abnormal
Other deep veins: >1.0 seconds abnormal
Worsens with standing position
Indicates valve incompetence

keyTakeaways: Tests patency between compression and probe
Must evaluate reflux in standing position

topics.title: Venous Valve Function
topics.quickSummary: Competent valves allow unidirectional flow toward heart. Incompetent valves allow reflux >0.5-1.0 seconds leading to venous hypertension.
clinicalPearls: Competent valves allow unidirectional flow toward heart
Flow moves from superficial to deep system through perforators
Valves close due to hydrostatic pressure preventing retrograde flow

sections.title: Normal Valve Function
sections.content:
Competent valves allow unidirectional flow toward heart
Flow moves from superficial to deep system through perforators
Valves close due to hydrostatic pressure preventing retrograde flow
Close rapidly (<0.5-1.0 seconds)

sections.title: Incompetent Valves
sections.content:
Reflux duration >0.5-1.0 seconds
Retrograde flow toward feet
Ineffective calf muscle pump
Increased venous stasis and pooling
Elevated venous pressure

keyTakeaways: Competent valves: unidirectional flow toward heart
Flow from superficial to deep via perforators

topics.title: Hydrostatic Pressure
topics.quickSummary: Weight of blood column. Zero at heart level in all positions. Standing at ankle: +100mmHg. Standing at head: -30mmHg.
clinicalPearls: Weight of blood column in vessels
Proportional to height of blood column
Zero at heart level in all positions
Pressure increases below heart, decreases above heart

sections.title: Principles
sections.content:
Weight of blood column in vessels
Proportional to height of blood column
Zero at heart level in all positions
Changes with body position

sections.title: Values
sections.content:
Supine: hydrostatic pressure = 0mmHg everywhere
Standing at heart level: 0mmHg
Standing at ankle: +100mmHg
Standing at head: -30mmHg
Pressure increases below heart, decreases above heart

keyTakeaways: Hydrostatic pressure = weight of blood column

topics.title: Ambulatory Venous Pressure
topics.quickSummary: Normal: drops to ~30mmHg with walking. Abnormal (incompetent valves): remains ~100mmHg. This leads to chronic venous insufficiency.
clinicalPearls: Calf muscle pump decreases venous pressure with walking
With incompetent valves: remains at ~100mmHg (standing pressure)
Pressure does not drop adequately with exercise

sections.title: Normal AVP
sections.content:
Lowest pressure during exercise
Normal ambulatory pressure: ~30mmHg
Calf muscle pump decreases venous pressure with walking
Pressure drops from 100mmHg (standing) to 20-30mmHg (walking)

sections.title: Abnormal AVP
sections.content:
With incompetent valves: remains at ~100mmHg (standing pressure)
Pressure does not drop adequately with exercise
Leads to venous hypertension
Causes chronic venous insufficiency symptoms

keyTakeaways: Calf muscle pump drops pressure from 100→30mmHg
Leads to venous hypertension and CVI
Failure to drop pressure causes symptoms

categories.title: Venous Anatomy
categories.description: Deep, superficial, and perforator venous anatomy with positioning

topics.title: Deep Venous System
topics.quickSummary: Carry 85-90% of venous return. Located beneath muscle fascia. Include CFV, femoral, popliteal, tibial veins.
clinicalPearls: Carry majority of blood back to heart (85-90%)
Include: CFV, femoral, popliteal, tibial veins

sections.title: Deep Vein Characteristics
sections.content:
Carry majority of blood back to heart (85-90%)
Accompanied by arteries
Located beneath muscle fascia
Include: CFV, femoral, popliteal, tibial veins
Contain valves to prevent reflux
Primary route for venous return

topics.title: Superficial Venous System
topics.quickSummary: GSV and SSV. Located above muscle fascia. Carry 10-15% of return. GSV evaluated standing. SSV evaluated seated.
clinicalPearls: Evaluated with patient standing (preferably on stool)
Leg rotated outward for medial aspect access
Most common site for venous insufficiency
Runs from medial ankle to saphenofemoral junction
Evaluated with patient seated at bed edge, legs dependent
Joins popliteal vein at knee (saphenopopliteal junction)

sections.title: Great Saphenous Vein (GSV)
sections.content:
Great Saphenous Vein (GSV)
Evaluated with patient standing (preferably on stool)
Leg rotated outward for medial aspect access
Most common site for venous insufficiency
Runs from medial ankle to saphenofemoral junction
Joins CFV at groin

sections.title: Small Saphenous Vein (SSV)
sections.content:
Small Saphenous Vein (SSV)
Evaluated with patient seated at bed edge, legs dependent
Runs along posterior calf
Joins popliteal vein at knee (saphenopopliteal junction)
Variable anatomy

sections.title: General Characteristics
sections.content:
Located above muscle fascia
Carry 10-15% of venous return
Connect to deep system via perforators
Common sites for varicose veins

keyTakeaways: GSV: evaluated standing, medial leg, joins CFV at groin
SSV: evaluated seated, posterior calf, joins popliteal

topics.title: Perforators & Patient Positioning
topics.quickSummary: Perforators connect superficial to deep system. Flow superficial→deep normally. DVT: supine/semi-erect. Insufficiency: MUST be standing.
clinicalPearls: Connect superficial to deep venous system
Flow from superficial to deep during muscle relaxation
Flow from deep to superficial during muscle contraction (normal)
Incompetent perforators allow reflux from deep to superficial
Contribute to varicose veins when incompetent

sections.title: Perforator Veins
sections.content:
Connect superficial to deep venous system
Flow from superficial to deep during muscle relaxation
Flow from deep to superficial during muscle contraction (normal)
Incompetent perforators allow reflux from deep to superficial
Contribute to varicose veins when incompetent

sections.title: DVT Evaluation Positioning
sections.content:
Supine or semi-erect
Semi-erect increases intra-abdominal pressure
Decreases venous outflow
Veins more easily visualized when distended

sections.title: Insufficiency Evaluation Positioning
sections.content:
Standing position mandatory
Patient on stool if possible
Maximizes hydrostatic pressure
Better visualization of reflux
Some labs use reverse Trendelenburg

categories.title: Venous Testing
categories.description: Compression technique, Doppler assessment, and DVT detection

topics.title: Compression Technique for DVT
topics.quickSummary: PRIMARY method for DVT detection. Complete compression = patent. Partial/no compression = DVT. Compress every 1-2cm.
clinicalPearls: Complete compression = vein completely collapses = patent
Use adequate pressure but not excessive

sections.title: Compression Principles
sections.content:
Primary method for DVT detection
Complete compression = vein completely collapses = patent
Partial/no compression = thrombus present = DVT
Compress every 1-2cm along vein length
Use adequate pressure but not excessive

sections.title: Transmural Pressure
sections.content:
Flattened veins with low volume: low transmural pressure
Low transmural pressure = more resistance to flow, LESS resistance to compression
Circular veins with higher volume: high transmural pressure
High transmural pressure = less resistance to flow, MORE resistance to compression
Distended veins harder to compress
Semi-erect positioning distends veins for better visualization

keyTakeaways: Low transmural pressure = easier to compress

topics.title: Doppler Assessment Techniques
topics.quickSummary: Evaluate spontaneity, phasicity, augmentation, and reflux. Loss of phasicity suggests proximal obstruction.
clinicalPearls: Assess if flow is present without augmentation
Should be present in large veins (CFV, femoral, popliteal)
Calf veins may not show spontaneity normally
Absence in large veins suggests obstruction

sections.title: Spontaneity
sections.content:
Assess if flow is present without augmentation
Should be present in large veins (CFV, femoral, popliteal)
Calf veins may not show spontaneity normally
Absence in large veins suggests obstruction

sections.title: Phasicity
sections.content:
Evaluate respiratory phasicity
Flow should vary with respiration
Loss of phasicity suggests proximal obstruction
Different pattern in upper vs lower extremities

sections.title: Augmentation
sections.content:
Distal compression increases flow
Tests patency between compression and probe
Brisk response = normal
Absent/blunted = obstruction or valve incompetence

sections.title: Reflux
sections.content:
Release of compression or Valsalva
Duration >0.5-1.0 seconds = abnormal
Indicates valve incompetence
Must be evaluated in standing position

keyTakeaways: Spontaneity in large veins (CFV, femoral, popliteal)

topics.title: DVT Detection & Critical Findings
topics.quickSummary: Non-compressible vein = DVT. Lower/upper extremity DVT = CRITICAL. Free-floating thrombus tail = CRITICAL (high PE risk).
clinicalPearls: Free-floating thrombus tail (not adhered to wall) = CRITICAL - high embolism risk

sections.title: Positive DVT Findings
sections.content:
Non-compressible vein = DVT
Loss of spontaneous flow
Loss of respiratory phasicity
Absent augmentation response
Echogenic material (thrombus) within lumen
Vein distension
Collateral vessels

sections.title: Critical Findings
sections.content:
Lower extremity DVT = CRITICAL
Upper extremity DVT = CRITICAL
IVC thrombus = CRITICAL
Hepatic vein thrombus = CRITICAL
Free-floating thrombus tail (not adhered to wall) = CRITICAL - high embolism risk

categories.title: Venous Disease
categories.description: DVT, chronic venous insufficiency, and calf muscle pump dysfunction

topics.title: Acute vs Chronic DVT
topics.quickSummary: Acute: fresh thrombus, distended vein, CRITICAL. Chronic: organized thrombus, may recanalize, collaterals present.

sections.title: Acute DVT
sections.content:
Fresh thrombus
Echogenic to anechoic
Vein distension
Non-compressible
No flow on color Doppler
Loss of respiratory phasicity
CRITICAL FINDING

sections.title: Chronic DVT
sections.content:
Old, organized thrombus
More echogenic
Vein may be smaller (scarred)
Partial recanalization possible
Thickened vein walls
Collateral vessels present

keyTakeaways: Chronic: organized, more echogenic, may be smaller

topics.title: Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI)
topics.quickSummary: Incompetent valves cause elevated ambulatory venous pressure (stays ~100mmHg vs normal 30mmHg). Leads to edema, skin changes, ulcers.
clinicalPearls: CVI: remains at ~100mmHg or higher with walking

sections.title: Pathophysiology
sections.content:
Incompetent valves allow reflux
Ambulatory venous pressure remains elevated
Normal: ~30mmHg with walking
CVI: remains at ~100mmHg or higher with walking
Leads to venous hypertension
Causes skin changes, edema, ulcers

sections.title: Ultrasound Findings
sections.content:
Reflux >1.0 seconds in deep veins
Reflux >0.5 seconds in superficial veins
Dilated, tortuous veins
Varicose veins
Perforator incompetence
Normal venous volume <150mL (increases with CVI)

sections.title: Clinical Signs
sections.content:
Leg swelling/edema
Skin pigmentation changes
Lipodermatosclerosis
Venous stasis ulcers
Heaviness, aching, fatigue in legs

topics.title: Calf Muscle Pump
topics.quickSummary: Normal: muscle contraction propels blood toward heart, pressure drops to ~30mmHg. Dysfunction: pressure decreases only slightly.
clinicalPearls: Venous pressure drops with ambulation to ~30mmHg
Causes: muscle wasting, obstruction, incompetent valves
Venous pressure decreases only slightly with ambulation

sections.title: Normal Function
sections.content:
Muscle contraction compresses veins
Propels blood toward heart
Valves prevent reflux
Venous pressure drops with ambulation to ~30mmHg
Efficient emptying and refilling

sections.title: Dysfunction
sections.content:
Causes: muscle wasting, obstruction, incompetent valves
Venous pressure decreases only slightly with ambulation
Refill time significantly shortened
Ineffective venous return
Venous pooling and stasis

keyTakeaways: Normal: contraction propels blood toward heart
Normal: pressure drops to ~30mmHg with walking
Dysfunction: muscle wasting, obstruction, incompetent valves
Results in venous pooling and stasis

categories.title: Arterial Testing
categories.description: ABI, segmental pressures, PVR, and exercise testing

topics.title: Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)
topics.quickSummary: ABI = ankle pressure / brachial pressure. Normal: 0.9-1.3. <0.9 = arterial disease. <0.4 = critical limb ischemia.
clinicalPearls: Ankle and brachial pressures equal or ankle slightly higher
Normal: ankle pressure same or higher than arm at rest
Exercise: pressures remain same or increase slightly
Exercise causes ankle pressure to drop with arterial disease
Reduced ABI indicates peripheral arterial disease

sections.title: Normal ABI
sections.content:
ABI = 0.9 - 1.3 (normal)
Ankle and brachial pressures equal or ankle slightly higher
Normal: ankle pressure same or higher than arm at rest
Exercise: pressures remain same or increase slightly

sections.title: Abnormal ABI
sections.content:
ABI <0.9 = arterial disease
ABI <0.5 = severe PAD
ABI <0.4 = critical limb ischemia
With stenosis: ankle pressure drops
Exercise causes ankle pressure to drop with arterial disease
Reduced ABI indicates peripheral arterial disease

sections.title: Calculation
sections.content: ABI = Highest ankle pressure / Highest brachial pressure

keyTakeaways: With PAD: ankle pressure drops with exercise

topics.title: Segmental Pressures & PVR
topics.quickSummary: Segmental pressures identify stenosis location. Gradient >20mmHg = significant. PVR measures volume changes - dampened waveform indicates proximal disease.
clinicalPearls: Pressure gradient >20mmHg between segments = significant stenosis

sections.title: Segmental Pressures
sections.content:
Identify location of arterial stenosis
Pressures measured at multiple levels
Compare adjacent segments
Pressure gradient >20mmHg between segments = significant stenosis

Levels: Upper thigh, Above knee, Below knee, Ankle, Metatarsal/toe

sections.title: Pulse Volume Recording (PVR)
sections.content:
Pulse Volume Recording - measures volume changes in limb segment

Normal: Rapid upstroke, Sharp systolic peak, Dicrotic notch present, Normal amplitude, Waveform mirrors arterial waveform

Abnormal: Reduced amplitude indicates stenosis, Delayed upstroke, Rounded peak, Loss of dicrotic notch, Dampened waveform suggests proximal disease

keyTakeaways: PVR normal: rapid upstroke, sharp peak, dicrotic notch
PVR abnormal: dampened, delayed upstroke, no dicrotic notch

topics.title: Exercise Testing
topics.quickSummary: Normal: ankle pressure stable/increases with exercise. PAD: ankle pressure DROPS with exercise (arterioles already maximally dilated).
clinicalPearls: Flow increases 3-5x resting flow with exercise
Ankle/brachial pressures same or mildly increased after exercise
Arterioles dilate to meet muscle oxygen demand
With stenosis: arterioles already dilated at rest
Cannot further reduce resistance with exercise
Muscles cannot increase flow to meet demand

sections.title: Normal Exercise Response
sections.content:
Flow increases 3-5x resting flow with exercise
Ankle/brachial pressures same or mildly increased after exercise
Arterioles dilate to meet muscle oxygen demand
Resistance drops, flow increases
Quick recovery to baseline

sections.title: Abnormal Exercise Response (PAD)
sections.content:
With stenosis: arterioles already dilated at rest
Cannot further reduce resistance with exercise
Ankle pressure drops with exercise
Muscles cannot increase flow to meet demand
Ischemic symptoms occur (claudication)
Prolonged recovery time

keyTakeaways: Normal: ankle pressure stable or increases
PAD: arterioles already maximally dilated at rest
PAD: cannot further dilate with exercise
PAD: ankle pressure DROPS with exercise

categories.title: Physics & Instrumentation
categories.description: Doppler principles, angle correction, aliasing, indices, and equipment

topics.title: Doppler Principles & Angle
topics.quickSummary: Doppler angle must be <60°. At 90°: no shift detected. At 0°: maximum shift. Frequency shift proportional to velocity and cos(angle).
clinicalPearls: Doppler effect: frequency shift when sound reflects from moving object
Flow toward transducer = positive frequency shift (above baseline)
Flow away from transducer = negative frequency shift (below baseline)
Frequency shift proportional to blood velocity

sections.title: Basic Doppler Principles
sections.content:
Doppler effect: frequency shift when sound reflects from moving object
Flow toward transducer = positive frequency shift (above baseline)
Flow away from transducer = negative frequency shift (below baseline)
Frequency shift proportional to blood velocity
Angle dependency critical for accuracy

Doppler Equation: Frequency shift = (2 × velocity × transmitted frequency × cos angle) / speed of sound

sections.title: Angle Correction
sections.content:
Doppler angle should be <60 degrees (ideally 45-60°)
At 90°: cos(90°) = 0, no Doppler shift detected
At 0°: cos(0°) = 1, maximum Doppler shift
Larger angles = greater error in velocity calculation
Angle correction cursor must be parallel to vessel wall/blood flow

sections.title: Angle Errors
sections.content:
Improper angle = inaccurate velocity calculations
Most common cause of velocity measurement error
Angles >60° exponentially increase error
Angle correction line must align with flow direction

keyTakeaways: Angle cursor must be parallel to flow

topics.title: Aliasing & PRF
topics.quickSummary: Aliasing occurs when velocity exceeds Nyquist limit (PRF/2). Solutions: increase PRF, decrease frequency, shift baseline.
clinicalPearls: Appears on opposite side of baseline

sections.title: Aliasing Description
sections.content: Occurs when velocity exceeds Nyquist limit (PRF/2)

sections.title: Color Doppler Aliasing
sections.content:
Mosaic pattern
Color reversal
Appears as turbulence
Post-stenotic turbulence commonly causes aliasing

sections.title: Spectral Doppler Aliasing
sections.content:
Waveform wraps around baseline
Peak velocities cut off
Appears on opposite side of baseline

sections.title: Solutions
sections.content:
Increase PRF (scale)
Decrease frequency (use lower frequency transducer)
Increase Doppler angle (with caution, <60°)
Shift baseline
Use continuous wave Doppler for very high velocities

sections.title: PRF
sections.content:
Higher PRF = higher velocities can be measured
Lower PRF = better sensitivity to slow flow
Nyquist limit = PRF / 2
Increase PRF to eliminate aliasing
Decrease PRF to see slow venous flow better

keyTakeaways: Aliasing when velocity exceeds Nyquist limit (PRF/2)
Solutions: increase PRF, decrease frequency, shift baseline

topics.title: Spectral Broadening & Bandwidth
topics.quickSummary: Spectral broadening = widening of waveform. Laminar: narrow, clear window. Turbulent: wide, filled window.
clinicalPearls: Improper sample volume location (too close to wall)

sections.title: Spectral Broadening
sections.content:
Widening of spectral waveform, filling of spectral window

Causes:
Stenosis (most common pathologic cause)
Tortuosity
Improper sample volume location (too close to wall)
Increased sample size (gate too large)
Bifurcations (normal)
Turbulent flow

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.content:
Laminar flow = narrow bandwidth, clear spectral window
Turbulent flow = wide bandwidth, filled spectral window
Degree of broadening suggests severity of disturbance

sections.title: Bandwidth
sections.content:
Narrow bandwidth = laminar flow, single velocity
Wide bandwidth = turbulent flow, range of velocities
Increases at stenosis
Increases at bifurcations

keyTakeaways: Laminar flow: narrow bandwidth, clear window
Turbulent flow: wide bandwidth, filled window
Causes: stenosis, tortuosity, improper sample volume

topics.title: Acceleration Time (AT)
topics.quickSummary: Time from onset of systole to peak velocity. Longer in ICA than extremities. Increases distal to severe stenosis.
clinicalPearls: ICA/cerebral vessels: longer AT than high resistance vessels
AT increases in extremities as distance from heart increases
Measured more easily with increased sweep speed
AT increases distal to significant stenosis
Decreased cardiac output increases AT bilaterally
Used to differentiate inflow from outflow disease

sections.title: Definition & Normal Values
sections.content:
Time from onset of systole to peak systolic velocity

ICA/cerebral vessels: longer AT than high resistance vessels
AT increases in extremities as distance from heart increases
Measured more easily with increased sweep speed

sections.title: Abnormal Values
sections.content:
AT increases distal to significant stenosis
Decreased cardiac output increases AT bilaterally
Used to differentiate inflow from outflow disease
Prolonged AT suggests proximal stenosis

keyTakeaways: AT = time from onset to peak systolic velocity
Measured more easily with increased sweep speed

topics.title: Resistive Index (RI) & Pulsatility Index (PI)
topics.quickSummary: RI = (PSV-EDV)/PSV. PI = (PSV-EDV)/mean velocity. Both NOT dependent on angle. If EDV=0, RI=1.0.
clinicalPearls: Values increase with distance from aorta

sections.title: Resistive Index (RI)
sections.content:
Formula: RI = (PSV - EDV) / PSV

Normal Values:
Extremity arteries: 0.6-0.8
Organ vessels: <0.6
If EDV = 0, then RI = 1.0

Uses:
Evaluates tissue resistance (renal parenchyma, liver, transplants)
Demonstrates resistance changes from stenosis/occlusion
Distal occlusion causes increased resistance proximally = high RI
Not dependent on angle

sections.title: Pulsatility Index (PI)
sections.content:
Formula: PI = (PSV - EDV) / mean velocity

Normal Values:
Organs: usually <1.5
Brain: <1.0
CFA: >5.0
Popliteal artery: >8.0
Values increase with distance from aorta
Higher in extremities than organs

Uses:
Compares PSV-EDV difference to average velocity
Measures variability in blood velocity during cardiac cycle
Distinguishes inflow from outflow disease
Not dependent on angle

topics.title: Bernoulli Effect & Flow Patterns
topics.quickSummary: Bernoulli: velocity increase = pressure decrease. Laminar: parabolic profile. Plug: flat profile. Turbulent: chaotic.
clinicalPearls: Slow blood = more pressure on vessel walls
Fast blood (at stenosis) = less pressure on vessel walls
Reduced pressure at stenosis with increased velocity
After stenosis: velocity decreases, pressure increases

sections.title: Bernoulli Effect
sections.content:
Principles:
Total fluid energy remains constant
Pressure energy + kinetic energy = constant
Velocity increase = pressure decrease
Velocity decrease = pressure increase

Clinical:
Slow blood = more pressure on vessel walls
Fast blood (at stenosis) = less pressure on vessel walls
Reduced pressure at stenosis with increased velocity
After stenosis: velocity decreases, pressure increases
Explains pressure drop across stenosis

sections.title: Laminar Flow
sections.content:
Concentric layers of flow
Parabolic velocity profile
Center fastest, edges slowest
Narrow spectral bandwidth
Clear spectral window
Normal in straight vessels

sections.title: Plug Flow
sections.content:
All layers same speed
Flat velocity profile
Occurs in systole in large vessels
At branch origins
Proximal to stenosis

sections.title: Turbulent Flow
sections.content:
Disrupted, chaotic flow
Random velocities and directions
Wide spectral bandwidth
Spectral broadening
Filled spectral window
Post-stenotic turbulence
Eddy currents and vortices

topics.title: Equipment & ALARA Principle
topics.quickSummary: ALARA = As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Linear array for carotids/extremities. Cannot thermally sterilize transducers (destroys piezoelectric elements).
clinicalPearls: Linear array: extremities and carotids (5-10 MHz)
Curved/phased array: abdominal and large habitus (2-5 MHz)

sections.title: ALARA Principle
sections.content:
As Low As Reasonably Achievable
Use lowest power settings possible
Limit exam times
Reduce ultrasound exposure
Especially important for obstetric exams

sections.title: Transducers
sections.content:
Linear array: extremities and carotids (5-10 MHz)
Curved/phased array: abdominal and large habitus (2-5 MHz)
Cannot be thermally sterilized
Heating above Curie point destroys piezoelectric elements
Cavicide wipes for most probes
Cidex for endocavity probes
NO iodine or alcohol cleaners (damages matching layer and adhesives)

sections.title: Presets
sections.content:
Carotid preset for carotid exams
Lower extremity arterial preset
Lower extremity venous for DVT
Lower extremity venous for insufficiency
Using wrong preset degrades image and extends exam time

keyTakeaways: ALARA: use lowest power, limit exam times

topics.title: Energy Types & Vessel Resistance
topics.quickSummary: Kinetic = motion energy (KE=½mv²). Potential = pressure energy. Resistance proportional to 1/radius⁴ (Poiseuille's law).
clinicalPearls: Varies with mass and velocity squared (KE = ½mv²)
Greater mass or velocity = more kinetic energy
Converts to kinetic energy during flow

sections.title: Kinetic Energy
sections.content:
Energy of motion
Varies with mass and velocity squared (KE = ½mv²)
Greater mass or velocity = more kinetic energy
Dominant in flowing blood

sections.title: Potential Energy
sections.content:
Stored energy
Pressure energy distending vessels
Like compressed spring
Converts to kinetic energy during flow

sections.title: Gravitational Energy
sections.content:
Stored energy related to elevated position
Hydrostatic pressure component
Changes with body position
Zero at heart level

sections.title: Vessel Resistance
sections.content:
Small changes in vessel radius = most significant changes in flow
Resistance proportional to 1/radius⁴ (Poiseuille's law)
Increased vessel radius = dramatically decreased resistance
Vessel length also affects resistance but less dramatically
Blood viscosity affects resistance

keyTakeaways: Small radius changes = large resistance changes
